text: The survey stakes went in on a Thursday, little orange flags marching right through the middle of the hydrangeas Marguerite had planted the summer we moved in. I stood at the kitchen window with my coffee going cold and counted them. Eleven. Our neighbor, Mr. Okafor, had been perfectly polite about it, had even brought over a printout of the fence design, cedar, six feet tall, very tidy. I told him it was fine. What else was I going to tell him? That my wife used to lean over that hedge every morning to hand him tomatoes, and that for thirty years the gap between our yards had been the place where the two households talked? She has been gone since March. The tomatoes are gone too; I never managed to water them. I went out after lunch and knelt in the wet grass beside the hydrangeas, my knees complaining, and dug up as many as I could fit in buckets. I don't know where I will put them. The bare patch of dirt looked like a missing tooth. When the hammering started on Monday I closed the window and sat down in her chair and did not get up for a long while.

Priya read the note twice before folding it back into its envelope. Her neighbor, Ruth, was selling the house and moving into a care home in the spring, and her son wanted a fence up first, to make the lot easier to list. Would Priya mind sharing the cost? There was a sketch of a fence line drawn in shaky blue ballpoint, and at the bottom Ruth had written, almost as an afterthought, Thank you for everything, dear. Priya sat on the back step for a long time with the paper resting on her knees. Through the gap in the old lilac bushes she could see Ruth's bird feeder, empty now, swinging a little in the wind. Every winter afternoon for six years the two of them had stood on either side of those lilacs, complaining about squirrels, swapping library books, saying nothing important at all. Priya's throat ached. She wanted to walk over and knock, but her legs felt too heavy to stand. Instead she went inside, found her checkbook, and wrote the amount slowly, her handwriting wobbling on the zero. Then she put the kettle on and forgot about it until it had boiled itself half dry.

"Just a low one," Grandpa Teodor said, "waist high. So the new people's dog doesn't wander." He said it lightly, but his eyes stayed on the line of string he was pulling taut between two pegs, and his hands were not quite steady. I was twelve and had come to help, mostly by holding things. The new people were nice enough. They had moved into the Lindqvist house next door after Mrs. Lindqvist died, and they had already torn out her rose garden and laid sod over it, flat and green and blank. Grandpa didn't say anything about the roses. He just kept measuring, then measuring again, as if the numbers might come out different. Around noon he sat down on an upturned bucket and rubbed his face with both palms and stayed like that, hunched, for so long that I started to worry. "She used to bring me lemonade at about this time," he finally said, his voice thin and far away. I didn't know what to say, so I went inside and made some, too sour, and he drank the whole glass without complaining and then just held the empty cup.

Every morning for nine years Hamid had walked across the strip of grass between his house and the Brennans' to collect their newspaper when they were away, to return a rake, to borrow eggs. Now there was a letter from the Brennans' lawyer in his hand, formal and cold, citing a boundary survey and their intention to erect a fence along the legal line. Not a word from Colleen herself. Not since the argument about the tree roots last autumn, which he'd thought had blown over. He set the letter on the hall table and stood there with his coat half off, one sleeve dangling. The house was very quiet. His daughter had moved to Vancouver; his wife worked late. He realized, with a slow sinking in his chest, that the Brennans had been the people he talked to most. He went to the window. Colleen was in her yard, hanging laundry, and for a moment he lifted his hand to wave. She didn't look up. He let his hand drop and stood there until the light changed and the room grew dim around him.

I found out about the fence from the contractor, not from Dana. He knocked on my door to ask if I knew where the water line ran, and I said, what fence? and he looked embarrassed for me. Dana and I used to share coffee on the porch steps every Saturday, her kids running back and forth through both our yards like it was one big field. Then she got remarried and things got quieter, and quieter, and now apparently there would be boards. I told the contractor I didn't know about the water line. After he left I sat on the steps anyway, the way I used to, mug in my lap. The kids' old soccer ball was still wedged under my azaleas, faded almost white. I didn't move it. When the posts went in I watched from behind the curtain, every thud landing somewhere under my ribs. By evening there was a clean pale wall where her kitchen window used to be, and I couldn't see the light she always left on over the sink. I went to bed early and lay there listening to the house tick.

Old Mr. Castellanos had asked the young couple next door for one thing when they proposed the fence: could they leave a little gate in it, near the fig tree, the way it had always been. They'd smiled and nodded and said they'd think about it. Now the fence was finished, tall and seamless, the fig tree cut neatly in half by the boards, and there was no gate. He stood in his slippers looking at it, holding the small basket he used for figs. On his side hung three or four green fruits, not yet ripe. On the other side, he knew, were all the good branches, the ones that got the afternoon sun, the ones his late brother had grafted in 1987. He reached up and touched one of the leaves poking over the top of the fence, rubbing it between his fingers until it gave off that green, milky smell. His eyes stung. He told himself it was the sap. Then he went back inside, set the empty basket on the counter, and sat at the table without turning on the light, listening to the neighbors laughing on their new patio.

The envelope had the property management logo in the corner, and Lucinda knew before she opened it. Sixty days' notice. The building had been sold; the new owners intended to renovate. She read it standing by the mailboxes in the lobby, then read it again in the elevator, then sat down on the edge of her bed still wearing her coat. Twenty-two years in this apartment. Her son had learned to walk on these floorboards, wobbling from the radiator to the couch. Her husband had painted the kitchen that awful mustard color and she had never repainted it, not even after he was gone, because it was his mistake and she liked having it. She looked around at the pencil marks on the doorframe, the crack in the bathroom tile shaped like Italy, and something in her chest just gave way, slowly, like a step that's been rotting for years. She did not cry. She sat with the letter in her lap until the radiator started clanking, the way it did every evening at six, and the sound was so familiar that she had to press her hand flat against her mouth.

I read the landlord's letter on the bus home, and by the time I reached my stop I'd missed it and had to walk back eleven blocks in the drizzle. Rent going up by four hundred a month, effective August. It wasn't a surprise exactly. Everyone on the block had been getting them. But I'd let myself believe Mrs. Adeyemi, who owned the building, liked me enough to make an exception. I'd fixed her gutter. I'd carried her groceries. The letter wasn't even signed by her; it came from some company in another state. I let myself in and didn't turn on the lights. The little window over the sink looked out onto the courtyard with the one scraggly cherry tree, and I stood there looking at it with my wet jacket dripping onto the linoleum. I did the math in my head three times and it never came out any different. I'd have to leave. The cherry tree would bloom next spring for somebody else. I sat down on the kitchen floor with my back against the cabinets, too tired to find a chair, and listened to the rain until it got dark.

Mateo held the letter out to his wife without a word. Inés took it, read it, and lowered herself slowly onto the arm of the sofa. The lease would not be renewed. The landlord's daughter was getting married and needed somewhere to live. The tone was friendly, apologetic even, which somehow made it worse. Their twins were asleep in the next room, in the bunk bed Mateo had built into the alcove, the one with the stars painted on the ceiling above it. Inés kept smoothing the paper against her knee, smoothing and smoothing as if she could press the words flat enough to disappear. "The school," she said finally, her voice barely there. "They just made friends." Mateo nodded. He went to the doorway of the boys' room and leaned against the frame, watching their small shapes under the blankets, one foot sticking out. He couldn't bring himself to go in and tuck it back. His shoulders had dropped somehow, like a coat slipping off a hanger. Behind him he heard Inés fold the letter into quarters, then eighths, then smaller still, until it would not fold anymore.

The letter said the landlord would be entering the unit on the fourteenth to assess its condition prior to the end of the tenancy. The end of the tenancy. Wen had signed the paperwork herself three weeks ago, but seeing it typed out made it real in a way her signature hadn't. She had lived in the little studio over the bakery for eight years, since the divorce, since she had shown up in this town with two suitcases and no plan. Now her knees hurt on the stairs and her daughter wanted her closer, in a city where she knew no one. That evening she wandered from the window to the bookshelf to the window again, picking things up and putting them back. The chipped blue mug from the market. The postcard from her sister, curling on the fridge. The smell of bread drifted up through the floorboards, warm and yeasty, the way it had every evening for eight years, and Wen sat down heavily on the bed, pressing the heels of her hands into her eyes. Downstairs someone laughed, and the oven door banged, and she stayed sitting there long after the smell had faded.

"It's just a letter," my roommate Jonah said, but he didn't sound like he believed it either. The landlord was converting the house into short-term rentals. We had until the end of the month. I'd been here four years, the longest I'd stayed anywhere since I left home, and the attic room with the slanted ceiling was the first place that had ever felt like mine. I'd painted the window frame green. I'd taped my nephew's drawings up along the beam. That night I lay on the mattress and looked at the drawings in the streetlight, a purple dog, a house with smoke curling out the chimney, a stick figure labeled AUNTIE in shaky capitals. My chest felt like someone had set a stack of books on it. I kept thinking about all the small things I would never do here again: hear the pipes knock when Jonah showered, step over the loose stair, watch the cardinal that came to the gutter every morning. I didn't pack. I didn't even get up to brush my teeth. I just lay there, listening to the house settle around me, trying to memorize the sound of it.

The notice was taped to every door in the building, so at least Mr. Dimitriou knew he wasn't being singled out. Demolition, it said. Eighteen months. Tenants would receive relocation assistance. He peeled it off carefully, the tape tearing a little strip of paint with it, and carried it inside to the kitchen table, where he set it down beside the photograph of Eleni. They had moved here in 1971, newlyweds, when the neighborhood was full of bakeries and Greek was spoken on every stoop. One by one the bakeries had closed, and one by one the neighbors had died or gone to their children in the suburbs, and Eleni had gone too, four winters ago. Now the building. He looked at the notice for a long time, then got up and went to the window. Across the street the old café was a phone shop now. He watched people hurry past with their heads down, none of them looking up. His hand found the windowsill and rested there, on the spot where the paint was worn smooth from fifty years of elbows, his and hers.

The board flipped from DELAYED to CANCELLED at 9:40, and a low groan rippled through Gate 23. Anjali didn't groan. She just sat very still with her phone in her lap, the screen still lit up with her brother's last message: Hurry, he's asking for you. The next flight was at six the next morning. The agent at the desk was kind, said she was sorry, said there was nothing she could do. Anjali thanked her. Her voice came out small and polite, as if from somewhere far away. She walked back to her seat, past a family sharing a bag of chips, past a businessman shouting into his earpiece, and sat down with her coat still on. Outside the big windows the planes sat in the rain, lights blinking, going nowhere. She thought about her father in the hospital bed in Pune, about how he used to hold her up on his shoulders to watch the planes take off when she was small. She pulled her knees up and wrapped her arms around them and rested her forehead there, and stayed like that while the terminal emptied out around her.

I had the little wrapped box in my carry-on, a wooden train I'd spent two weeks hunting down, because Theo had seen one in a picture book and pointed at it every time we video-called. His fourth birthday party was at three. My flight was supposed to land at noon. At gate B7 the delay kept growing, an hour, then three, then a mechanical issue, then a crew timing out. By two I knew I wasn't going to make it. My ex-wife texted a photo of the cake, a dinosaur with green frosting, and then, a minute later, He keeps asking when Daddy's coming. I read it and put the phone face down on my knee. I watched a toddler across the aisle stomp in circles in light-up sneakers, her father pretending to chase her. My jaw ached from clenching it. Around four I opened the box and took the train out and just held it, turning the little painted wheels with my thumb, feeling ridiculous and unable to stop. When they finally called boarding at seven I was the last one to stand up.

Mrs. Halvorsen was eighty-three and had never flown alone before. Her granddaughter had printed everything out for her in large type, the gate, the connection, the phone numbers, and clipped it all together with a pink paperclip. Now the screen said her connecting flight was delayed four hours, which meant she would miss the dinner, the one her grandson had planned to celebrate his graduation. She held the papers tightly on her lap and watched the crowds stream past, so fast, everyone knowing where they were going. A young man in an airline vest bent to ask if she needed anything, and she said no, thank you, with a small smile that didn't reach her eyes. She opened her purse and took out the card she had written for Anders, read it over again, put it back. Then she unwrapped the cheese sandwich she had packed and took one bite and couldn't manage any more. She wrapped it back up very neatly, folding the wax paper corners just so, and sat with it in her hands, looking at the clock above the gate as the minutes crept by.

"Delayed again," the announcement said, and I just closed my eyes. I'd been trying to get home for Abuela's funeral for thirty-one hours by then. First the storm in Chicago, then the missed connection, now this. The service was at ten the next morning, and I was sitting on the carpet in Denver with my back against a charging station, my phone at four percent, watching the snow pile up on the wings outside. My cousin had sent a photo of the church, the white flowers already in place. I couldn't look at it for long. My eyes kept sliding off it, to the floor, to the stranger's suitcase next to me. I kept thinking about Abuela's hands, the way they smelled of onions and lotion, the way she tapped my cheek twice before she let me go every visit. The last time, I'd been in a hurry. I'd pulled away early. I pressed the back of my head against the hard metal of the charging station until it hurt, and stared up at the ceiling lights, and waited for the next announcement, already knowing what it would say.

The flight to Accra was delayed overnight, and the airline handed out hotel vouchers that nobody seemed to want. Kwame took his and then didn't go. He stayed in the half-dark terminal, cleaners pushing their machines in long humming loops across the tile, and sat by the window with his duffel bag between his feet. He was supposed to be at his mother's house by morning. She'd been cooking for two days, she'd told him on the phone, groundnut soup, the kind he liked, and she'd laughed in that bright way of hers that had gotten thinner each time they spoke. The doctors said months, maybe less. Every hour he wasn't there felt like something being poured out onto the floor. He tried to call her and it went to voicemail, her recorded voice cheerful and out of breath, and he listened to it twice and hung up without leaving a message. Around three a.m. a cleaner asked if he was all right. Kwame nodded. He had his hand pressed flat over his mouth and couldn't take it away to answer.

I'd timed everything so I'd land with an hour to spare before my best friend's wedding. Lea and I have known each other since we were six; I was meant to give the toast. I had it on index cards in my blazer pocket. Then the plane sat on the tarmac in Lisbon for three hours with a hydraulic problem, and then we were all herded back to the gate, and by the time they rebooked me the ceremony was already over. Someone posted a video. Lea walking down the aisle, crying, laughing, looking around once at the front row as if she was searching for someone. I watched it about six times in a plastic chair by Gate 14, my thumb hovering over the screen. Her maid of honor gave a toast in my place. It was fine. People laughed. I took out my index cards and read my own toast silently, mouthing the words, the joke about the treehouse, the line about her mother. My eyes blurred halfway through. I put the cards back in my pocket and pressed my palm over them, as if they could keep something warm.

The doctor's office called on a Tuesday and asked Rosalind to come in instead of discussing the results over the phone. She knew what that meant. She drove there carefully, both hands on the wheel, noticing everything: the woman walking a beagle, the bakery's new sign, how ordinary the street looked. Dr. Mbeki was gentle. She drew a little diagram. She used the word treatment several times and the word cure not at all. Rosalind nodded along, asked sensible questions, even thanked her. Then she sat in her car in the parking lot for forty minutes without starting the engine. Her granddaughter's drawing was still taped to the dashboard, a lopsided sun and two stick figures holding hands, GRANMA AND ME in crayon. She looked at it until the colors swam. She thought about the garden she had just planted, the bulbs that wouldn't come up until April. Her hands lay limp in her lap, palms up, and for a while she didn't seem to have the strength to lift them. When she finally drove home she took the long way, past the school, slowly, just to see the children running out.

I knew from the nurse's face, actually, before the doctor even came in. She was too careful with me, too soft, offering me a cup of water I hadn't asked for. The test confirmed it: the pregnancy wasn't viable. There would be no heartbeat. The doctor talked about next steps, about how common it was, about how it wasn't anything I'd done. I heard about half of it. I kept staring at the poster on the wall, a cheerful cartoon uterus with a speech bubble, and thinking how strange it was that someone had drawn it, that someone had thought it was a good idea. Daniel squeezed my hand so hard the ring dug into my finger. In the car neither of us said anything. At home I went straight to the spare room, where we'd started stacking things: a secondhand crib, still in pieces, a bag of tiny socks my sister had sent. I sat down on the floor among them. Daniel stood in the doorway, then came and sat beside me, and we stayed there with our shoulders touching until the room went gray.

Ibrahim had been told to expect the results by Friday, and on Friday the email came: his hearing loss was permanent and likely to progress. The audiologist recommended he begin learning to lipread. He read the email at his desk at the music school, where he'd taught violin for twenty-six years. Down the hall a student was sawing through a scale, slightly flat on the F sharp. A week ago he'd have winced. Now he had to lean toward the door to hear it at all. He closed the laptop gently and sat looking at his own violin in its open case, the varnish worn pale where his chin had rested for half a lifetime. He reached out and touched one string, lightly, and leaned close, and it was there, faint and woolly, like a sound heard through water. His shoulders slumped forward. When his next student knocked, a timid eleven-year-old named Pilar, he had to ask her twice to repeat herself. She did, louder, and he forced a smile and said, of course, let's begin, and his voice cracked on the last word.

The results were good, mostly. That was what the specialist said, smiling, turning the screen toward Nkechi so she could see the clean scans. Mostly. The cancer was gone. But the treatment had done what they'd warned it might do, and the second test, the one she'd almost forgotten about, confirmed that she would not be able to have children. Nkechi nodded and said she understood. She shook the doctor's hand. Her husband hugged her in the hallway, laughing with relief, saying we did it, we did it, and she let him hold her and patted his back. In the elevator she watched the numbers count down and felt nothing, a wide flat nothing, like a field after snow. It was only later, at home, when she opened the hallway closet and saw the box of baby clothes her mother had been saving since the eighties, that something buckled in her. She sank down onto the floor with the door still open. The little yellow cardigan was on top. She didn't touch it. She just looked at it, and kept looking, and couldn't make herself close the door.

My father opened the envelope at the kitchen table while I pretended to wash dishes. I watched him in the reflection of the window. He read the page once, then took his glasses off and polished them on his shirt, slowly, the way he does when he's buying time. "Well," he said. Just that. The scans showed the memory loss was what the doctor had suspected. Early stage, the letter said, as though that made it gentler. Dad set the paper down and lined it up with the edge of the table, squaring the corners. "Your mother always said I'd forget my own head," he said, and tried to laugh, and the laugh came out wrong, broken in the middle. I turned off the tap. I didn't trust my voice. I dried my hands and sat down across from him, and he looked at me with such a lost, apologetic expression that I had to look at the tablecloth instead. We sat there not talking while the fridge hummed. Then he reached across and patted my hand, twice, the way he used to when I was a kid with a fever.

Corinne opened the patient portal at her desk on her lunch break, which she knew was a mistake even as she clicked. The biopsy report loaded line by line. She didn't understand half the words, but she understood malignant. She read it three times. Around her the office went on: someone microwaving fish, the copier jamming, Gerald laughing too loudly at something on his phone. She closed the browser. She opened a spreadsheet and stared at it, the cells blurring into a gray grid. Her sandwich sat untouched beside the keyboard. At two o'clock she went into a meeting and sat through it, nodding when other people nodded, writing nothing on her notepad. Afterward, in the bathroom, she ran cold water over her wrists and looked at herself in the mirror and thought, You're forty-one, and felt her face start to crumple and caught it, held it, the way you'd catch a glass about to fall. She went back to her desk. She didn't call anyone. She kept thinking of her sister's voice and how it would change when she heard, and she couldn't bear to be the one who changed it.

Ms. Aldana set the exam face down on Joon-ho's desk, and he knew from the way she didn't meet his eyes. He waited until she'd moved on before he turned it over. A red 48, circled twice. He had studied for this one. He'd stayed up until two every night for a week, made flashcards, gone to the tutoring center even though the bus took forty minutes. He looked at the circled number and felt something heavy settle in his stomach, like he'd swallowed a stone. Around him people were comparing scores, groaning or cheering. He slid the paper into his folder without reading the comments. At lunch he sat at the end of the table and peeled his orange very slowly, one strip at a time, and didn't eat it. His mother had written GOOD LUCK on a sticky note inside his lunch bag that morning, with a little drawing of a star. He found it again under the orange and smoothed it flat with his thumb, and his eyes went hot, and he folded the note into his pocket before anyone could see.

I got the chemistry final back and it was a C minus, which isn't the end of the world, I know, except it meant I wouldn't get into the summer program at the university. I'd told everyone about the program. My grandmother had already told her whole church group. I sat in the back row of the lab with the paper in my hands, staring at the long rows of red X's next to the stoichiometry problems, and the room felt very far away, like I was looking at it from the bottom of a pool. Mr. Feldman said a few people could see him after class if they had questions. I didn't go. I didn't think I could get a sentence out without my voice cracking. On the walk home I kicked a pinecone the whole length of Maple Street and didn't feel like kicking it at all. My grandmother was on the porch, waving. I made myself wave back. I went up to my room and lay face down on the bed with my shoes still on and let the paper fall onto the floor somewhere below me.

When Professor Lindgren handed back the essays, Amara's had only a few lines of comments at the end. Competent but derivative. Lacks a genuine argument. B minus. She read it walking across the quad in the cold and slowed until she was barely moving, students streaming around her on both sides. She had written about her mother's village, about the songs the women sang while pounding cassava, and she had thought, while writing it, that it was the truest thing she'd ever made. Derivative. She sat down on a bench even though it was wet and felt the cold seep through her jeans and didn't get up. Her phone buzzed: her mother, asking how the essay went. Amara typed fine and deleted it, typed good and deleted that too. Pigeons shuffled around her feet, hopeful. She had nothing for them. She folded the essay in half, then in half again, and held it pressed between her palms, and watched her breath cloud and vanish in front of her face until the bell rang for her next class and she still didn't stand.

The spelling test had a sticker on top, but it wasn't a star. It was a little frowning cloud, which Miss Patterson used when you got less than half right. Eli was seven and had practiced with his dad every night at the kitchen table, writing the words over and over until his hand cramped. Because. Friend. Through. He had gotten because wrong again. He stared at the cloud sticker. All around him kids were showing each other their stars, and Mia had a gold one, and she held it up so everyone could see. Eli put his test inside his desk and closed the lid very quietly. At recess he didn't run to the swings. He sat on the bottom step by the door and drew circles in the dust with a stick, around and around, until the circles turned into a deep groove. When his dad picked him up he climbed into the car without saying hi and stared out the window, chin trembling. His dad looked at him in the mirror and asked, softly, if he wanted to stop for ice cream, and Eli shook his head.

I'm forty-six and I went back to school to finish the nursing degree I quit when the twins were born. Pharmacology is the hardest class I've ever taken. Last night I studied at the kitchen table until midnight while the dishwasher ran and the dog snored on my feet. This morning Professor Osei handed back the midterm and I'd failed it. Not barely. Fifty-one percent. The girl next to me, maybe twenty, got a ninety-four and said, Oh my god, I didn't even study. I smiled at her. I don't know why. My face just did it. Then I went out to my car and sat with the paper on the steering wheel and the engine off and looked at all the drug interactions I'd mixed up, and thought about the twins, who are in college now and think it's so cool that their mom's going back too. I don't know how I'll tell them. My hands felt cold and slow. I sat there until the parking lot attendant tapped on the window to ask if I was okay, and I said yes, sorry, yes, and started the car, and just kept sitting.

Vikram had needed a seventy on the bar prep practice exam to keep his scholarship, and he'd gotten a sixty-four. He read the email in the library, in the corner carrel he'd used every day for two years, and then sat back slowly in the chair as if someone had let the air out of him. On the wall of the carrel, scratched into the wood by some long-ago student, were the words YOU CAN DO THIS. He had always found it funny. Now he looked at it for a long time. He thought about his father driving taxis through two decades of night shifts in Toronto so that someone in the family could do this. He thought about the phone call he would have to make. His throat closed up just thinking about it. He started packing up his books, then stopped halfway, a heavy casebook in his hands, and just held it against his chest. Outside the tall windows the sky was gray and low, and a few flakes had started to fall. He watched them drift down, landing and melting on the glass one at a time.

I almost didn't recognize Sophie. She was standing in front of the cereal, thinner, her hair cut short, and when she turned and saw me her face did something complicated before it settled into a smile. We'd been inseparable at nineteen. Then her brother died, and I didn't know what to say, so I said nothing, and kept saying nothing for eleven years. "Hey, stranger," she said. We hugged, awkwardly, around my cart. She asked about my job and I asked about hers, and we both answered in short tidy sentences, and all the while I could feel the thing I never did hanging between us like a smell. She said she had a kid now. She showed me a picture. A little boy with her brother's ears. My throat tightened so hard I had to look away at the price tags. "He's beautiful," I managed. She put her phone back. "Well," she said. "It was good to see you." I watched her push her cart toward the checkout and didn't follow. I stood in the cereal aisle holding a box I didn't want, reading the nutrition facts over and over.

Gustavo spotted him by the bananas: Raymond, his old partner from the fire station, the man who'd carried him out of the warehouse fire in '98. Raymond was leaning heavily on the cart, and as Gustavo got closer he saw the slackness on one side of his face, the careful shuffle. A stroke, maybe. Nobody had told him. "Gus," Raymond said, and his voice was slower than it used to be, the words thick. He grinned his old crooked grin, and it only went halfway. Gustavo gripped his shoulder and felt how thin it had gotten under the flannel. They talked for five minutes, about the Dodgers, about nothing. Raymond kept losing his place in a sentence and laughing it off. When his daughter came to collect him, Gustavo watched them go down the aisle, her arm hooked through his, and stood for a long time beside the bananas. A teenager stocking shelves asked if he needed help finding anything. Gustavo shook his head. He left his basket where it was, half full, and walked out to the parking lot and sat in his truck with his hands on the wheel.

It was the laugh that made me turn around in the frozen aisle, that big honking laugh I'd know anywhere. Nadia. We'd shared a dorm room our first year, shared everything, then drifted the way people do, Christmas cards, then not even those. She was with a man and two teenage girls, and she looked happy, really happy, and she hugged me hard and said, "Oh my god, look at you!" and introduced me to everyone. Her daughters were polite. Her husband shook my hand. Then they had to go, they were late for something, and she said we should get coffee, and I said absolutely, and we both knew we wouldn't. I watched them go out through the sliding doors, all four of them talking at once. I was holding a single frozen dinner. One fork's worth of lasagna. I looked down at it and something in me just quietly sank. I put it in my basket anyway. At the register the cashier asked how my day was going, and I opened my mouth to say fine and found I couldn't get the word out, and just nodded instead.

Mrs. Abernathy recognized Constance's voice before she saw her, two aisles over, asking a clerk where they kept the tinned peaches. They had been best friends for forty years, through husbands and children and a falling out over something so small neither of them could now remember it. Mrs. Abernathy rounded the corner and there she was, smaller than she remembered, holding a list in a shaky hand. "Connie," she said. Constance looked at her politely, pleasantly, the way you'd look at a stranger who'd been kind enough to hold a door. "Hello," she said. "Do I know you?" A younger woman, a carer perhaps, stepped close and murmured an apology. Mrs. Abernathy's hand went to her chest. She opened her mouth and closed it. "No," she said finally, softly. "I must have been mistaken." She found the tinned peaches herself and placed them in Constance's basket, and Constance thanked her very nicely. Then Mrs. Abernathy stood in the aisle among the canned goods while her own cart sat abandoned, and pressed her gloved fingers to her lips, and did not move for a long time.

I saw Marcus in the checkout line ahead of me, and for a second I was seventeen again, the two of us skateboarding behind this very store, sharing stolen sodas on the loading dock. He turned and saw me and his face lit up, then dimmed when he saw what I was buying: the cheap stuff, the generic everything, a single can of coffee. He was wearing a suit. He'd made it out, gone to law school, the whole thing. I hadn't made it anywhere. I was still in the same town, working at the plant, which was closing in the spring. He asked what I'd been up to. I said, "Oh, you know." He said we should catch up properly and handed me a business card, thick and smooth, embossed. I held it and nodded. When he left, I stood there turning the card over in my fingers while the cashier rang up my things. Outside, it had started to drizzle. I walked out past the loading dock and the spot where we used to sit was fenced off now, and I stood looking through the chain link with the rain dripping off my hood.

Yuki recognized her across the produce section by the way she tilted her head while choosing tomatoes, pressing each one gently with her thumb. Hana. They had grown up two doors apart in Osaka and moved to this country the same year, as girls, clinging to each other through every unfamiliar thing. Then Hana married, and moved to another state, and the phone calls got shorter and further apart. Now here she was. Yuki called her name and Hana looked up and her eyes filled immediately. They held each other right there by the tomatoes. Hana was only in town for her mother's funeral. She was flying out tomorrow. "I meant to call you," she said, and Yuki said, "I know, me too," and they both stood there with their hands clasped, not knowing how to fit thirty years into the few minutes before Hana's husband came looking for her. When she'd gone, Yuki picked up one of the tomatoes Hana had been holding. It was still faintly warm from her hand. Yuki held it for a long moment, then set it carefully back on the pile and walked out without buying anything.

The engine coughed twice and died on the shoulder of Route 9, and Bernadette just let the car roll to a stop and sat there. She didn't put the hazards on right away. She didn't reach for her phone. It was her husband's old Buick, the one she'd kept driving after the funeral because selling it felt like selling a piece of him. He'd always been the one who knew what the noises meant. He'd tilt his head and listen and say, Fan belt, or, That's nothing, don't worry. Now there was no one to tilt their head. She looked at the dashboard, at the little dent where he used to tap it with his knuckle for luck, and her chest went tight. Cars whipped past, rocking the Buick slightly with their wind. She finally turned the hazards on and the clicking filled the silence, steady as a clock. She called work and said she'd be late, her voice flat and level. Then she called the tow truck. Then she just sat there with her hands folded in her lap, watching the hazard light pulse orange against the guardrail, waiting.

My car died on the bridge at 7:15 in the morning, and I'd only had the job for three weeks. Third job this year. I'd promised myself this one would stick. I sat there with the engine ticking and horns going off behind me, and I didn't even get angry, I just felt the energy run out of me like water out of a sink. My supervisor had already warned me once about being late. I called and got voicemail. I left a message, apologized too many times, heard my own voice shrinking as I talked. The tow truck took an hour. The driver was friendly, chatty, and I couldn't find anything to say back. When he dropped me at the garage, the mechanic told me it was the transmission. Two thousand dollars. I had about four hundred in the bank. I thanked him and walked out and sat on the curb outside the garage, next to a puddle with an oil sheen on it, and watched the rainbow colors swirl. My phone buzzed. It was my supervisor. I watched it ring until it stopped, and then I sat there some more.

Rashida's car shuddered, lurched, and gave up three miles from the hospital where she worked night shifts. She coasted onto the shoulder and turned the key again. Nothing but a click. She rested her forehead against the steering wheel. It was the third breakdown this month, and she knew, with a dull certainty, that she couldn't fix it again; there was nothing left to fix it with. Her children's school photos were tucked into the sun visor. Her son's was from last year, before he stopped smiling for pictures. She looked at it in the yellow dome light, at his gap-toothed grin, and thought about how tired she'd been lately, how short with him, how she'd missed his band concert because of a double shift. Rain began to tap on the roof, slow at first, then steadier. She didn't call anyone yet. She just pulled her coat tighter and watched the windshield blur, drop by drop, until the streetlights were soft smears of gold, and let herself sit there for five minutes, ten, before she had to be the person who handled things again.

"Come on," Felix whispered, turning the key again, "come on, please." The old Volvo wheezed and went silent. He was on the way to work, but also, more importantly, on the way to drop his daughter at her mother's for the week, and Tilly had been quiet the whole drive, looking out the window. Now she looked at him with her big serious eyes. "Are we stuck?" "Just for a bit, kiddo." He called his ex-wife. She sighed and said she'd come get Tilly herself. When her car pulled up behind them twenty minutes later, Tilly unbuckled and climbed out with her little purple backpack, and turned at the last second to wave. Felix waved back. Then the other car pulled away and he was alone on the shoulder with the hood up and her juice box still in the cupholder, half finished, the straw bent. He picked it up and held it. The cardboard was still cool. He sat back in the driver's seat with the door open and the morning traffic roaring past, and he didn't call his boss, didn't call a tow, just sat there holding a juice box.

Mr. Sato had driven the same route to the print shop for thirty-four years, and the van had carried him for nineteen of them. When it finally died, it did so quietly, in the left lane at a red light, the engine simply stopping as if it had decided it was done. He pushed it to the curb with the help of two teenagers who happened to be passing. They didn't seem to know what to say to an old man. He thanked them with a little bow. Then he stood beside the van and laid his hand flat on its warm hood, the paint chalky and faded, the logo of his shop peeling off the side. The shop was closing in a month anyway. His son had found him a buyer for the building. There had been no reason to fix the van, and now there would be no reason to drive it. He stood there with his palm resting on the metal until it cooled beneath his hand. A bus went by. He watched it go and didn't wave it down, didn't move at all, just stood beside his van on the side of the road.

I heard the bang, then felt the steering go loose, and I limped onto the gravel on the side of the county road. Flat tire, and the spare was flat too, because of course it was. I'd meant to fix it. I'd meant to fix a lot of things. I was on my way to the office to clear out my desk; they'd let me go the week before, after nine years. My plan had been to slip in early and slip out before anyone saw me. Now I was standing in a field of corn stubble with my phone at nine percent, watching crows pick at the furrows. I called my brother. He said he'd come when he could. I sat on the guardrail. A truck went by and the driver lifted two fingers off the wheel, the way people do out here, and I tried to lift mine back but by the time I did he was gone. The empty box I'd brought for my things sat on the passenger seat. I could see it from where I sat. I looked at it for a long time, flattened at the corners, and felt the whole morning just sag.

The clock on the microwave said 1:47. Esperanza had stopped pretending to read hours ago and was sitting at the kitchen table in her robe, her phone face up in front of her, the last message she'd sent to Lucas still unanswered: Are you okay? Just let me know. She knew he was probably fine. That was almost the worst part. He was probably fine, and he just didn't think to tell her, didn't want to, the way he didn't want to tell her anything these days. He used to tell her everything. When he was nine he'd followed her from room to room narrating every detail of his Minecraft world until she begged for mercy. Now his door stayed closed and he answered her questions with one syllable, and she'd find out about his life sideways, from other parents. She picked up his old Lego astronaut from the windowsill where it had stood for years and turned it over in her fingers. The fridge hummed. A car passed outside and slowed, and her heart lifted, and it didn't stop. She set the astronaut down very gently and kept waiting.

I've been sitting in the dark living room since midnight. Curfew was eleven. Destiny's phone goes straight to voicemail, which means it's off, which means she turned it off. Not dead battery; she charges it religiously. She turned it off so I couldn't reach her. I keep thinking about last week, when I said something cruel about her new friends, and she looked at me like I was someone she'd never met. I wanted to take it back the second I said it. I didn't. Now I'm on the couch with her baby blanket in my lap; I don't even know why I got it out of the closet. It's pilled and soft and it still smells faintly of the cedar chest. I keep rubbing the satin edge between my thumb and finger, the way she used to when she was falling asleep. The house is so quiet I can hear the clock in the hall. At 1:30 headlights finally sweep across the wall. Her key turns. She walks past the living room doorway without looking in, and I hear her bedroom door shut, softly, and I sit there holding the blanket.

Graham sat on the front steps with a mug of tea gone cold beside him, watching the street. His son Owen was supposed to be home by midnight. It was now well past one. He wasn't truly worried; Owen had texted at eleven, Running late, with no explanation. What weighed on him was something else. Tomorrow Owen was leaving for the army, and this was meant to be their last night, and Graham had cooked his favorite, the lamb with rosemary, and set two places at the table. Owen had eaten fast and left with his friends, and the second plate of dessert was still sitting in the fridge under cling film. Graham hadn't said anything. He hadn't known how. He looked up at the streetlight, moths circling it, and thought about teaching Owen to ride a bike on this exact stretch of pavement, running behind him with one hand on the seat, then letting go. His eyes blurred. When the taxi finally pulled up at half past one, Graham stood up too quickly, wiped his face with his sleeve, and pretended he'd just come out for air.

It was after two when I finally heard the car door slam outside. I'd been sitting at the top of the stairs in the dark for an hour, the way I used to sit when Kenji was little and had nightmares and I'd wait to hear if he'd call out again. He came in quietly, shoes in hand, and didn't see me. He went to the kitchen and opened the fridge and stood in its light, and I saw his face. He'd been crying. My son, sixteen and taller than me now, standing in the fridge glow with red eyes and a bitten lip. I wanted to go down. I wanted to put my arms around him the way I would have five years ago. But he'd made it so clear, so many times, that he didn't want that from me anymore. So I sat on the step with my hands clasped between my knees, holding my breath, and listened to him drink a glass of water and rinse it and climb the back stairs to his room. His door clicked shut. I stayed where I was, my legs gone numb beneath me, staring at the line of light under it until it went out.

Every Friday night Halima did the same thing: made a pot of mint tea, sat by the front window, and waited for Samir to come home. He was seventeen and had a job now, washing dishes at a restaurant across town, and he came home at all hours smelling of grease and bleach, too tired to talk. Tonight it was nearly one when she saw him walking up the path, his shoulders hunched, his hood up. He came in and she said, "There's tea," and he said, "I'm okay, Mama," and went straight to his room. She poured herself a second cup she didn't want. His school had called again that afternoon. He'd stopped going to his morning classes; he was sleeping through them. He was giving her most of his paycheck for the rent, and she had taken it, because she'd had no choice. She sat with the cup warming her hands and looked at the framed photo on the shelf: Samir at ten, in a science fair ribbon, grinning, holding a model volcano. She kept looking at it until her tea went cold and the street outside fell completely silent.

The porch light was on, the way it always was when one of the kids was out, and Walter sat beneath it in the wicker chair with a blanket over his knees. Nora was nineteen now, home from college for the summer, and technically she didn't have a curfew. But he couldn't sleep until she was in. He never could. He listened to the crickets and the far-off highway and thought about how quiet the house had been this past year without her, how he'd kept walking past her empty room and stopping in the doorway, looking at the posters she'd left on the wall. In two weeks she'd go back, and then after that, she'd said tonight at dinner, she might take a job in Seattle. She'd said it lightly, buttering her bread. He'd said, That's great, sweetheart, and meant it, and felt something drop through the floor of him. Now he pulled the blanket up and watched the dark road. When her headlights finally appeared at the end of the street, he got up and switched off the light and went inside before she could see him waiting.

Ms. Fairbanks closed the door behind Tomasz, which she never did, and he understood before he sat down. Budget cuts. The whole design team. She was very sorry. She had fought for them. He nodded at all the right places and asked about severance and health insurance in a steady voice, and she slid a folder across the desk. He took it. On the way back to his cubicle he walked past the little kitchen where, every Wednesday for six years, he'd brought in pastries from the Polish bakery near his flat. His coworkers were all at their desks now, very quiet, staring at their screens. Somebody had already heard. Nobody looked at him. He sat down and looked at his monitor, at the half-finished project he'd been so pleased with that morning, the logo for the children's hospital. He saved it. He didn't know why. Then he opened his drawer and started taking out his things: the mug his daughter had painted, a spare tie, a stress ball shaped like a cat. He held the cat in his palm and couldn't make himself squeeze it.

My manager called me in on a Friday at four, which is never good, but it wasn't what I expected. She wasn't firing me. She was leaving. Diane, who'd hired me straight out of school when nobody else would, who'd taught me everything, who'd sat with me in the stairwell the day my dad died. Her husband had been transferred overseas. "I wanted you to hear it from me first," she said, smiling, though her eyes were wet. I said congratulations. I said how exciting. My voice sounded like someone else's, high and bright and wrong. She gave me a hug across the desk, which was awkward, and I laughed, and she laughed. Then I went back to my desk and opened an email I'd been working on and read the same sentence about quarterly projections maybe fifteen times. I kept looking over at her office, the light on, her silhouette moving behind the frosted glass. At six I packed up slowly and stood by the elevator and let two of them go by. When the third came I got in, and watched the doors close on the floor, and leaned my head back against the wall.

Ezekiel had been with the company for twenty-eight years when his new manager, a man half his age named Brody, called him in to discuss what he called a transition plan. There were charts. There was talk of streamlining. There was the phrase early retirement package, said so kindly it took Ezekiel a moment to understand what it meant. He sat with his hands folded on his knees and looked past Brody's shoulder at the window, at the parking lot below where his old Chevy sat in the same spot it always had, under the one tree. He thought about all the Christmas parties, the retirement cakes he'd helped cut for other people, the cards he'd signed. He'd always imagined he would be the one choosing the day. "Take some time to think about it," Brody said. Ezekiel nodded. He stood up slowly, his knees aching, and thanked him, actually thanked him, then walked down the long corridor past the framed photos of company picnics. In one from 1998 he could see himself in the back row, grinning, his arm around a man who'd died two years ago.

I was called into the manager's office to be told I hadn't gotten the promotion. That was all. It went to Kristin, who'd been there a year and a half; I'd been there seven. My manager, Mr. Delgado, was nice about it, said I was invaluable where I was, said there'd be other opportunities. I said I understood. I said Kristin would do great. Then I went back to my desk and the afternoon just sort of sagged around me, like a tent with the poles pulled out. I had told my mother about the interview. She'd already started telling people. I'd told myself it was mine. I stared at the photo pinned to my cubicle wall, me and my mother at my college graduation, her in that ridiculous purple hat. She'd driven nine hours to be there. I unpinned it and looked at it closer and pinned it back crooked and didn't fix it. At five Kristin came by, glowing, and asked if I wanted to grab a drink to celebrate. I said I couldn't, I had plans. I went home and sat on the edge of the bathtub with my coat still on.

Mr. Whitfield, the store manager, had his reading glasses pushed up on his forehead and a stack of papers in front of him. "Sit down, Lupe," he said gently. She sat. He told her that corporate was closing the location at the end of the month. All forty employees. She had worked there since it opened, nineteen years ago, back when the parking lot was still dirt and the shelves smelled of fresh paint. She'd trained half the staff. She knew every regular by name, which ones wanted paper bags, which ones wanted to talk. She asked what would happen to Mrs. Dunleavy, who came in every Tuesday at ten for her prescriptions and her chat. Mr. Whitfield didn't have an answer. When she came out of the office the store was busy, carts rattling, the radio playing something cheerful and tinny. She went back to register four and smiled at the next customer and scanned his cereal and his milk. Her fingers knew the codes without looking. She said, Have a good day, and he said, You too, and she watched him go and blinked hard, twice.

Owusu had been looking forward to the meeting. He thought it was about the new project, the one he'd pitched. Instead his manager, Sandra, told him that the client had pulled out, and the project was cancelled, and the team that he had spent four months building, the team he'd fought to hire, would be broken up and reassigned. Nobody was losing their jobs; she wanted to make that clear. He thanked her for telling him in person. He walked out past the whiteboard in the corner still covered in their diagrams, arrows and boxes and little jokes in the margins, someone's cartoon of him in a superhero cape. He stopped in front of it. The marker had started to fade. He couldn't bring himself to wipe it off. At his desk his team messages were already lighting up, people asking what was going on, and he looked at the little circles with their faces in them and didn't type anything. He put his head in his hands. When the cleaner came by at seven, he was still sitting there, and the whiteboard was still full.

The box was labeled XMAS in my mother's handwriting, but underneath the tangled lights I found a bundle of letters tied with ribbon. They were from my father, written to her the year he worked on the oil rigs, before I was born. I sat down right there on the dusty floor of the attic, under the one bare bulb, and untied the ribbon. My darling Vera, the first one began, I counted the waves today and every one was a day closer. I didn't know he could write like that. The father I remembered was quiet, tired, a man who fell asleep in front of the television in his work boots. He died when I was fifteen and I never once heard him say anything soft. I read three letters and had to stop. My hands were trembling, and the paper was so thin I was afraid I'd tear it. Mom had been gone two years now, and the house was sold, and I had until Friday to empty it. I sat there in the dust with the letters in my lap and a cobweb in my hair and couldn't make myself stand up.

Behind a box of old tax returns, Aurelio found a shoebox, and in it a single letter in his own handwriting, dated thirty years earlier. He had been twenty-two. It was addressed to Benedetta, the girl he was supposed to marry before his family emigrated. He had written it the night before the ship, pages and pages, promising he would send for her. He had never sent it. He had told himself he would mail it from the new country, and then there had been work, and the language, and the years. And then a cousin's letter, mentioning in passing that Benedetta had married a baker from the next village. He sat on a trunk in the stuffy attic heat and unfolded the pages. The ink had faded to the color of weak tea. He read the line, I will never love anyone the way I love you, and pressed the back of his wrist hard against his mouth. Downstairs his wife was calling him for dinner. He folded the letter back along its old creases, very slowly, and put it in his shirt pocket over his heart, and sat a moment longer before going down.

I wasn't looking for anything; I was just trying to make room for the Christmas decorations. But there it was, in the bottom of my old school trunk: a letter from Callie, my best friend in high school, written the summer before senior year. It was full of exclamation points and inside jokes and plans for the trip we were going to take after graduation, to the coast, in her brother's van. We're going to see every lighthouse!!! she'd written, and drawn a little lighthouse with beams coming out of it. We never went. She got sick that winter, and by spring she was gone, and I'd boxed up everything that reminded me of her and pushed it to the back of the attic and tried, for twenty years, not to think about it. I sat cross-legged on the plywood floor and traced the little lighthouse with my fingertip. The roof creaked as the wind picked up. My chest felt hollowed out, scooped clean. I read the letter twice more, then held it against my knee and just let the attic go dark around me.

Siobhan found the letter in the pocket of her grandfather's old wool coat, which had been hanging in the attic since he died. It was addressed to her, in his cramped hand, and the date on it was the week before his death. She had been at university then, in the middle of exams, and hadn't come home in time. She sat down on the dusty floorboards to read it. It was short. He told her not to worry about coming, that he understood. He told her he was proud of her. He told her to look after her mother, and to keep the garden going, and that the secret to tomatoes was talking to them. At the end he had written, I'll miss our walks, love, and then the pen had trailed off, as if he'd gotten tired. Siobhan's breath came shallow and uneven. Nobody had given it to her. It had been sitting in a coat pocket for six years, waiting. She held the paper to her face and breathed in, as if it could still smell of his pipe, and it only smelled of dust.

Clearing out my mother's attic, I found a letter I had written to her when I was eight. I'd run away, briefly, to the end of the block, and left her this note on the kitchen table. In wobbly capitals it said: I AM LEEVING BECAUSE NOBODY LISENS. I WILL MISS THE CAT. LOVE DARIUS. She had kept it. Forty years. She'd kept it in an envelope with my name and the date written on the front, as if it were something important. I laughed at first, alone up there in the stale heat. Then the laugh caught in my throat and turned into something else. I thought of all the times I hadn't called back. The Sunday dinners I'd skipped. The last visit, when I'd been checking my phone the whole time and she'd asked me about my work and I'd given her short answers. She had listened to me my whole life, and I had kept that note's promise backward. I put my forehead down on the edge of the cardboard box and stayed like that, breathing in mothballs, until my brother called up the stairs asking if I was all right.

The letter was wedged between two picture frames in the far corner of the attic, and Mei-Lin almost threw it out with the rest of the paper. Then she saw the stamp: a red Chinese stamp from 1962. It was from her grandmother's sister, the one who had stayed behind. Mei-Lin's Mandarin was weak, but she could read enough. Elder sister, it began. I go to the river every evening and look in the direction you went. The writer asked whether they had arrived safely, whether there was rice, whether the children were well. She asked for a photograph. Mei-Lin looked at the envelope again. It had never been opened until now; the flap was still sealed at one corner. Her grandmother had never read it. Maybe she couldn't bear to. Maybe it had arrived after she'd stopped hoping. Mei-Lin sat back on her heels among the boxes, holding the thin blue paper in both hands, and pictured a woman standing alone by a river, every evening, for years. The light through the small round window had turned orange. She did not move to turn on the bulb.

I set six places at the table before I remembered, and then I stood there holding the sixth plate. Five. It was five now. Every year on the first Sunday of December, Gran's old friends came for dinner, and every year Pauline sat at the end nearest the window because she liked to watch the snow. She'd died in October. I put the plate back in the cupboard, very carefully, and the little chink it made against the others sounded too loud in the quiet kitchen. The roast was nearly done. The potatoes were boiling. I'd made Pauline's trifle, the one with too much sherry, because it was tradition and because I hadn't known what else to do. Now it sat in the fridge looking like a mistake. I wiped my hands on my apron and went to rearrange the chairs so the gap wouldn't show. It still showed. The doorbell rang, and I heard Agnes's cheerful voice in the hall, and I pressed my knuckles hard against my lips for a second and then went to answer it, smoothing my apron, putting on my face.

Ignacio stirred the mole sauce slowly, the way his mother had taught him, scraping the bottom so it wouldn't catch. It had taken him two days. Twenty-six ingredients. He'd toasted every chili himself, ground the seeds by hand, filled the whole apartment with smoke and the smell of cinnamon and chocolate. The guests were due at seven: his sister, her husband, their kids. The first family dinner since the funeral. He tasted the sauce from the wooden spoon and closed his eyes. It was close. It was so close. But it wasn't hers. Something was missing, some small thing she'd never written down because she'd never thought she would need to. He tasted it again, and again, and couldn't find it. His shoulders curved forward over the stove. The clock on the oven said 6:48. He set the spoon down on the counter and stood there with both palms pressed against the edge, head bowed, steam rising around his face so that he couldn't tell, after a moment, what was steam and what wasn't. When the buzzer went, he wiped his face on a dish towel and turned the heat down low.

My son and his new wife were coming for dinner, their first visit since the wedding, and I'd been cooking since noon. Lasagna, the kind with the béchamel, because it had always been Jamal's favorite. At five he texted: Hey Ma, Keisha's vegan now, so am I, hope that's ok! A heart emoji. I read it standing in the kitchen with oven mitts still on my hands. I looked at the lasagna through the oven window, the cheese just starting to bubble. I didn't know he'd changed. He used to tell me things like that. He used to call every Sunday; now it was once a month, if that. I took the mitts off and laid them on the counter, side by side, and pulled up a recipe for roasted vegetables on my phone, and my thumb was shaking a little as I scrolled. I had nearly everything. I started chopping. Carrot, onion, carrot. Every few minutes I looked over at the lasagna, cooling now on the stovetop, all that work. When the doorbell rang, I covered it with a dish towel so they wouldn't see it, and went to let them in.

Every Thursday for eleven years Birgit had cooked dinner for the book club, and tonight would be the last. The group was disbanding; too many members had moved away, or into homes, or simply stopped coming. Only three were left. She'd made the fish soup they always asked for, with saffron and the good bread from the market, and she'd set the table with her mother's linen, ironed that morning. Now she stood at the stove with the ladle in her hand and looked at the empty living room through the doorway, the circle of armchairs where once there had been twelve people arguing about Tolstoy over her soup. There were three chairs set out now. The others had gone to the basement. She'd carried them down herself, one by one, last week. The soup simmered and gave off its rich briny smell. She turned the burner down and pressed the back of her hand to her forehead and stood there in the warmth of the kitchen, very still, looking at the three chairs, until the knock came and she had to go and open the door.

I had wanted the evening to be perfect, because it would be the last time we'd all be together before Ana moved to Melbourne. I'd made the paella in the big pan, the one we'd bought on our honeymoon, the one I hadn't used since Miguel left. Saffron, chorizo, mussels. The kitchen smelled the way it did when we were all still a family. The kids were coming, all three of them, and Ana's boyfriend, and I'd laid out the plates and lit candles and even put on music. Then my youngest called: he was sick, couldn't make it. Then Ana texted that they'd be an hour late. I turned the heat down under the pan and sat on a stool by the stove, the wooden spoon still in my hand. The candles were already burning down, wax pooling on the tablecloth. I didn't blow them out. I sat and watched the rice, the steam, the little flames shivering every time the fridge kicked on. I kept thinking: this is the last time, and it's already slipping away, and I'm sitting here alone with a pan too big for anyone.

Rafferty was rolling out the dough for dumplings when his phone lit up on the counter. His old army friend, Pete, and Pete's wife were the guests, and they were thirty minutes away. Rafferty didn't pick up the phone right away. His hands were floury and he kept rolling, slowly, back and forth. It was the first time he'd seen Pete since they'd both come home, and he'd been planning this dinner for a month, practicing the dumplings because Pete's mother used to make them at the base on holidays. He finally wiped his hands and read the text. Pete couldn't come. Bad night. Sorry, man. Next time. Rafferty set the phone face down. He looked at the neat rows of dumplings on the tray, forty-two of them, pinched closed one by one, each a little crooked. The water was already boiling. He stood there in the steamy kitchen listening to it bubble, his floury hands hanging at his sides. After a while he turned the burner off and covered the tray with a clean towel and sat down at the table set for three.

The new apartment was clean and white and smelled of fresh paint, and Juliette hated how quiet it was. In her old place in Lyon the walls had been thin; she'd heard the neighbor's radio, the downstairs baby, the old man coughing across the hall. Here, in this city where she knew no one, there was only the hum of the fridge and the occasional siren far below. She sat on a box labeled KITCHEN because she hadn't unpacked the chairs. She had taken this job because it was a promotion, because everyone had said it was a wonderful opportunity. Her mother had cried at the train station. Now Juliette looked around at the stacked boxes and couldn't find the will to open even one. She got out her phone and scrolled to her sister's number and didn't call, because it was late there and Celine had the kids to put down. She put the phone away. Outside the big window the city lights went on and on, thousands of windows, and she didn't know a single person behind any of them. She pulled her knees up and rested her chin on them.

I spent the first night in the new apartment sleeping on the mattress on the floor, because the bed frame was still in pieces and I couldn't find the Allen key. The movers had left at six. My girlfriend had stayed back in Denver, because her job was there, because we'd decided we would try long distance, because we were mature and sensible people. I lay on my back and looked at the bare ceiling, a water stain shaped like a rabbit in one corner. I'd unpacked one thing: a mug she'd given me, with a bad pun on it about coffee. I'd put it on the empty counter and it looked ridiculous there all by itself. Around midnight I called her and she didn't pick up, which was fine, she'd said she would be asleep. I listened to her voicemail greeting anyway. Then again. My chest felt like it had a hole punched straight through it, a draft blowing in. The radiator ticked and clanked. I rolled over and pulled the comforter over my head, and it smelled like her laundry detergent, and that was worse.

Obinna carried the last box up three flights of stairs and set it down in the middle of the new studio, then just stood there, breathing hard, looking at the four walls. It was smaller than the photos had suggested. The window faced a brick wall. He'd moved here for graduate school, across an ocean, leaving his mother and his three younger sisters in Enugu, and the program had been everything he'd dreamed of for years. He'd pictured this moment. He'd pictured feeling something bright. Instead he felt hollowed out, scooped empty. He opened the box. On top, wrapped in a T-shirt, was the framed photo his sisters had given him at the airport, the four of them squeezed together, making silly faces, the youngest sticking out her tongue. He sat down on the floor with it. He propped it up against the wall and looked at it. Somewhere down the hall a door slammed and someone shouted in a language he didn't know. He stayed on the floor until the window went dark, and didn't turn on the light, and didn't unpack anything else.

The moving truck pulled away and I waved at it, which was stupid; the driver didn't wave back. Then I turned and went up into the apartment that was supposed to be my fresh start after the divorce. Two bedrooms, one for me and one for the kids every other weekend. The second bedroom had two little beds I'd assembled myself, with matching dinosaur bedspreads. It looked like a showroom. Nobody had ever slept in it. I sat on the edge of one of the beds and smoothed the bedspread with my hand, a green stegosaurus under my palm. Next weekend they'd come. Next weekend, and the one two weeks after that, and so on, a calendar of borrowed days. My throat burned. I'd hung their drawings on the fridge already, ones I'd taken from the old house: a rainbow, a spaceship, a family of four stick figures holding hands. I hadn't been able to look at that one too long. I lay back on the narrow bed with my feet still on the floor and looked at the glow-in-the-dark stars I'd stuck to the ceiling, which weren't glowing yet because it wasn't dark.

Mrs. Novak's new apartment was on the ground floor of an assisted living building in a city two hours from the town where she'd spent her whole life. Her son had picked it. It was very nice, he kept saying. There was a garden. There were activities. She stood in the middle of the small sitting room among her few remaining things, most of the furniture having been sold or given away, and looked at the picture rail where she would hang her husband's paintings. Only four of them had come. The rest had gone to an auction house. Her son kissed her cheek and promised to visit on Sunday and hurried out, checking his watch. Mrs. Novak sat down in her armchair, the one thing she had insisted on, and put her hands on its worn arms, feeling the familiar shiny patches where her fingers had rubbed the fabric for forty years. Through the wall she could hear a television, someone else's game show. Outside a woman she didn't know was pushing a walker along the path. Mrs. Novak watched her go by, and then watched the empty path.

Thabo unlocked the door to the new flat at eleven at night, after two flights and a long, confusing train ride, and found the electricity hadn't been turned on yet. He stood in the doorway with his suitcases and his phone flashlight, looking at the bare floorboards stretching into the dark. He'd taken the job in Glasgow because there was nothing for him in Johannesburg, because his father had pushed him, because everyone said he would be a fool to turn it down. He hadn't told anyone how much he had not wanted to go. He dragged the suitcases in and sat on one of them. It was cold, far colder than he'd expected for September, and he pulled his jacket tighter. His mother had packed a tin of rusks in his bag, he discovered when he opened it looking for a sweater. She hadn't told him. There was a note taped to the lid in her careful script: For when you are homesick. He held the tin on his lap in the dark, the phone light pointing up at the ceiling, and didn't open it, and didn't eat, and didn't sleep for a long while.

At mile twenty-five Leonie's legs felt like they belonged to someone else, but it wasn't the pain that made her eyes sting. It was the empty stretch of sidewalk by the bakery on Elm. Every year her father had stood exactly there, with a sign he'd made from a pizza box, GO LEO GO, and a thermos of terrible coffee he would try to hand her as she ran past. Every year she'd laughed and waved him off. This year there was just a fire hydrant and a woman she didn't know, clapping politely for everyone. Leonie kept running. Her breath came ragged and hitching, and it was hard to tell anymore what was from the race. She'd almost not entered. She'd entered because he would have been furious if she didn't. Her feet slapped the pavement, left, right. She passed the bakery and didn't look back at the hydrant. Somewhere ahead the crowd noise swelled toward the finish, cowbells and cheering, and she ran toward it with her face crumpled, tears and sweat running together down her neck, crossing the line without looking at the clock.

I knew around mile twenty-three that I wasn't going to qualify for Boston. I'd trained for eighteen months. Five a.m. runs in the dark, the ice, the shin splints, the hip that clicked. I'd skipped birthday parties and weddings and once, unforgivably, my niece's recital. All for one number on a clock. By the last mile I'd slowed to a shuffle. People were passing me, a man in a banana costume, a woman pushing a stroller. I could see the finish banner in the distance, bright and cheerful, and I couldn't make myself care. My calves were cramping. My chest felt heavy and dull, like I was carrying something in it. Volunteers held out cups of water and I took one and forgot to drink it. I kept thinking about all the mornings I'd lied to myself that this was worth it. The crowd was shouting, Almost there, you've got this, and I wanted to tell them, no, it's already gone. I crossed the line and someone hung a medal around my neck, and I walked to the edge of the barrier and sat down on the curb, holding it.

Kofi's coach had run the first twenty-five miles beside him in spirit, he liked to say, though in fact Coach Tremaine had died in the spring, three months before the race they'd planned together for two years. The last mile came up through the park, under the oak trees, and Kofi's lungs burned and his knees felt full of gravel. He'd written Coach's name on the back of his hand in marker. He looked at it now, the letters smeared with sweat, barely readable. He thought about the old man yelling at him on the track at six in the morning, Arms! Arms! Don't flap like a chicken! and a choked sound escaped him, half laugh, half something else. His pace slowed. A spectator shouted his bib number and he lifted a hand weakly. The finish line was there, finally, under the inflatable arch, and he made himself run the last hundred meters properly, arms pumping the way he'd been taught. Over the line, he stopped, bent double, hands on his knees, and stayed bent over long after his breathing had slowed, staring down at the smeared name on his hand.

The last mile was supposed to be the part where I'd feel something. That's what everyone told me. Shirin, you'll fly, the crowd will carry you. But my sister was meant to be running beside me. We'd signed up together after our mother died, a way to have something to train for, something to talk about besides hospitals. Then in August Farah got a job in Dubai and pulled out, and moved, and now we text maybe once a week, and the race was just me. I passed mile marker twenty-five and looked at the empty space to my left where she should have been. My legs were slow and leaden. The sun was glaring off the bay. Strangers yelled my name off my bib, Go Shirin!, and every time it felt like a small hand pressing on a bruise. I thought about how we'd planned to cross holding hands, how corny that would have been, how she'd have complained about the photo. I crossed alone, my arms at my sides. Afterward I sat on the grass wrapped in a foil blanket, crinkling, and didn't take a single picture.

By mile twenty-five Margaret was walking. Sixty-eight years old, her first marathon, and she'd promised her husband she would finish it. Not for herself; for him. He'd signed them both up two years ago, the day after his diagnosis, as a joke and also not a joke. They'd trained together for a year, slowly, until he couldn't anymore. Now she walked under the gray sky, the stragglers' bus crawling behind her, the crowds mostly gone home. A few volunteers were taking down the water tables. One of them, a young man with a beard, clapped for her as she passed and called out, Looking strong! She smiled at him and kept walking. In her pocket was his race bib, number 2214, folded in half. She touched it through the fabric now and then, like a worry stone. Her hip ached. Her feet were blistered. The finish line was half dismantled when she reached it, the clock still running, the numbers enormous and meaningless. She took out the folded bib and held it up as she stepped across, and her face crumpled, and she stood there a long time with it in her hand.

Every runner around Diego seemed to be smiling in that final mile, fists pumping, families leaning over the barriers shouting names. He looked for his parents in the crowd and didn't find them. He hadn't really expected to. His father had said, when Diego told him about the marathon, What's the point of running nowhere? and his mother had said nothing at all. His legs were heavy and his toes had gone numb an hour ago. He passed a little girl holding a sign that said RUN DADDY RUN with a drawing of a sneaker. He passed a group of college kids with cowbells. He passed an old couple holding hands, waving tiny flags. None of it was for him. He kept his eyes on the road ahead, the gray asphalt, the painted blue line he'd been following for twenty-five miles. Near the finish he checked his phone, just once, while he jogged. No messages. He put it back in the armband. He crossed the line with his head down, accepted a banana and a medal from a volunteer, and walked out through the exit chute toward the bus stop, alone.

I opened the back door for the third time and called her name into the dark. "Biscuit! Biscuit, come on, girl." Nothing. Usually she'd be scratching to come in by now, impatient for her bedtime treat. She was fourteen and mostly deaf and her hips were bad, and the vet had used the word soon at our last visit, which I'd chosen not to think about. I went out with the flashlight, my slippers soaking up the dew. The beam swept the lawn, the shed, the vegetable bed. I found her curled under the lilac bush at the far end, in the hollow where she liked to lie in summer. Her eyes were open. Her tail moved, once, when she saw me. She didn't get up.
