I knelt down in the wet grass beside her and put my hand on her side and felt how slow her breathing was, how shallow. "Okay," I whispered. "Okay, sweetheart." I set the flashlight on the ground, pointing at nothing, and lay down beside her under the bush, my cheek against her fur, and stayed there, cold and wet and not moving, all night.

Leilani stood at the kitchen window watching the yard, the ceramic water bowl in her hands. Max had gone out an hour ago. He always came back in ten minutes, nose pressed to the glass door, leaving smudges she pretended to be annoyed about. The gate was closed; she'd checked. She'd walked the fence line twice. She'd shaken the treat bag and listened for the jingle of his collar and heard only the wind in the gum trees. Her daughter was asleep upstairs. Max was really her daughter's dog, a birthday present three years ago, and they slept curled together every night. Leilani set the bowl down by the door, full, the way he liked it. Then she went outside again with the torch and walked the dark yard slowly, saying his name softly so as not to wake anyone, Max, Max, until the word didn't sound like anything anymore. She found the gap under the back fence then, freshly dug, the dirt still loose. She knelt down and put her hand in the hole. On the other side was only the road and the long dark.

My husband was the one who always let Rufus out and called him back in. That was his job. He'd stand on the porch and whistle, two notes, high then low, and Rufus would come bounding out of the hedge no matter what he'd been chasing. It's been eight months since the funeral. Tonight I let Rufus out at ten and he didn't come back. I called his name. I called it louder. I clapped. I rattled his bowl. Nothing. I stood on the porch in my cardigan, shivering, looking at the black shape of the hedge, and I realized I couldn't whistle. I'd never learned. I tried, and only air came out, a pathetic thin hiss. I sat down on the porch step with my arms wrapped around myself. I tried again. Air. And then, I don't know why, I just put my face in my hands. After a long time I heard rustling, and Rufus came trotting out of the dark, unhurried, his tail going. He pushed his wet nose into my neck. I held onto him far too tight, and he let me.

Old Mr. Kowalczyk had left the back door open so Duchess could come in when she was ready. That had been after supper. Now it was nearly midnight, and the cold air had crept through the whole kitchen, and her basket by the stove was still empty. He hadn't gone to look. He knew, the way you know some things without being told. She was sixteen. She'd barely eaten in a week. That afternoon she'd walked very slowly out to the apple tree and lain down in the leaves, and when he'd called her she'd only lifted her head. He sat at the kitchen table in his coat with the light off, looking out at the dark yard, at the shape of the apple tree against the sky. His tea had gone cold hours ago. Her lead hung on its hook by the door. Eventually he stood, his knees cracking, and took the old blanket from her basket and folded it over his arm, and found the flashlight in the drawer, and went out into the yard to go and sit with her under the tree.

Mina was nine and had been in charge of letting Pepper out before bed every night since summer. It was her job, her responsibility, the first one her parents had ever trusted her with. Tonight she'd opened the door and then gone to watch her show, and forgotten, and it was only when the show ended that she remembered. She ran to the back door. The yard was dark and empty. The side gate was hanging open; the latch had never worked right. She called Pepper's name so loud her voice cracked. Her dad came out, then her mom, and they walked up and down the street with flashlights, and Mina followed behind them in her pajamas and rain boots, not crying, holding her breath so she wouldn't. Her mom said, "It's not your fault, honey," in a gentle voice, and somehow that made it worse. When they got home without him, Mina went to Pepper's bed in the laundry room and lay down on it, curled up exactly the way he did, her face pressed into the blanket that smelled of dog, and didn't answer when they called her for bed.

The yard was quiet when I went out to call Hank in, too quiet. Usually he'd be barking at the possum that lived in the woodpile. I found him lying near the back fence, on his side, in the long grass. At first I thought he'd just stretched out in the last bit of sun. Then I saw how still he was. He was twelve. I'd raised him from a puppy, back when I was married and the kids were small and the yard was full of plastic toys and noise. He was the last thing left from those years, really. Everything else had gone. I knelt next to him in the grass and put my hand on his head, between his ears, where he liked to be scratched, and the fur was still warm. I didn't say anything. There wasn't anyone to say it to. The neighbor's kid was practicing trumpet two houses down, the same five notes over and over, wrong every time. I sat back on my heels with my hand on Hank's head and listened to the trumpet until the sun went all the way down.

Backstage, Esther tuned her cello for the fifth time even though it was already in tune. The concert hall was nearly full; she could hear the low roar of a few hundred conversations through the curtain. In the third row, seat C12, there would be an empty chair. She had bought the ticket for her teacher months ago, before the stroke, before the hospital, before the call last Thursday. Madame Laurent, who had taught her since she was six, who had smacked her knuckles with a pencil for sloppy bowing and then cried at her first recital. The program had her name printed in it, in small italics: This performance is dedicated to Hélène Laurent. Esther ran her thumb along the cello's scroll, over the tiny nick where she'd dropped it at twelve and Madame had pretended not to be furious. Her throat felt tight and narrow, like a reed. The stage manager touched her shoulder. Two minutes. She nodded and stood and lifted the instrument, heavier than usual, and walked out into the bright light, and did not look at the third row.

It was supposed to be our band's last show, and nobody had said it out loud yet, but we all knew. Jesse was moving to Austin. Tomasina was pregnant. I was going back to school. Eight years we'd been playing together, starting in Jesse's garage with a broken drum kit and a borrowed amp, and now here we were in a bar that could hold maybe a hundred, and about forty people had come. Most of them were friends. I sat on an amp in the back hallway restringing my guitar, slowly, taking too long with each string. Through the door I could hear Jesse laughing with someone, his big easy laugh, and I thought I would miss that sound more than anything. My fingers kept slipping on the tuning pegs. Tomasina came and sat beside me and didn't say anything, just leaned her shoulder against mine. We sat like that for a minute. Then the bartender poked his head in and said we were on, and we got up, and I picked up my guitar and it felt heavy as a door.

The piano was a Steinway, black and gleaming under the stage lights, and the auditorium was full of parents and teachers. Hyun-woo sat backstage in his rented tuxedo, its sleeves a little too long, and looked at the program in his lap. He was third. Chopin, the Ballade. He had practiced it every day for a year. His mother had always come to his recitals. She'd sit in the front row with her handbag in her lap and her eyes closed the whole time, swaying very slightly. This would be the first recital since she'd gone back to Korea, after the separation, after the long shouting nights. She'd said she would watch the livestream. He knew the time difference; it would be four in the morning there. He looked at his hands. They were cold. He pressed them between his knees to warm them, and stared at the scuffed floor, and tried not to think about whether she would set an alarm. When they called his name he stood, and walked out, and before he sat at the piano he looked once at the front row, where a stranger sat with a handbag.

I'd played this jazz club every Thursday for twenty-two years, and tonight was the last. The owner was selling the building. They were turning it into condos. I sat at the bar before the set, nursing a club soda, and looked around at the place: the water stain on the ceiling over table six, the photos of every musician who'd ever played here, curling in their frames, the tiny stage with the worn-out spot in the carpet where my left foot always rested. Sal, the bartender, slid a whiskey in front of me without asking. I didn't drink it. I just turned the glass slowly, watching the light move in it. The room was full tonight, fuller than it had been in years. People had come to say goodbye. Everyone kept patting my shoulder, saying things like, End of an era, and I kept saying, Yeah, yeah it is. My throat was thick. When it was time I climbed onto the stage and settled behind the keys, and put my left foot down on the worn spot, and sat there for a long moment before I could play the first chord.

Nobody in the church knew that Abigail was singing at her own mother's memorial. Well, everyone knew. But nobody understood that the hymn she'd chosen was the one her mother had sung to her every night when she was little, in the dark, off key and soft, so that Abigail had never been able to hear it since without feeling small and safe. She stood in the vestry with the sheet music, which she didn't need, crumpled slightly in her grip. Through the door she heard the organ, and someone coughing, and the low murmur of the congregation. Her aunt put her head in and whispered, "Are you ready, love?" Abigail nodded. She wasn't. Her throat felt swollen. She'd tried to practice last night and gotten through two lines before her voice gave out, and she'd sat on the floor of her childhood bedroom until midnight. She smoothed the sheet music flat against her skirt. She took one breath, then another, which came out shaky. Then she walked out into the aisle, past the lilies, past the photograph on its easel, and turned to face everyone.

Ravi had stopped playing the sitar for eleven years after his guru died. Tonight, at the community center, he was going to play again, at the request of the guru's grandson, who had organized a memorial evening. Ravi sat in a folding chair in the side room among stacked tables and a broken projector, the instrument across his lap. He touched the strings without plucking them. His fingers had grown stiff; the calluses had softened. He had been practicing for three weeks, and every night he could hear how far his playing had fallen from what it had been, and every night he could hear what his teacher would have said, the click of his tongue, the patient sigh. Through the wall someone was testing a microphone, one two, one two. Ravi bowed his head and closed his eyes. His shoulders were rounded, his breath slow and uneven. He thought of the old man's hands guiding his, decades ago, on a rooftop in Varanasi with the river below. When the grandson came to fetch him, Ravi stood, holding the sitar close against his chest, and did not trust himself to speak.

The box on the doorstep had a return address from a veterinary clinic in Sacramento, and Delphine didn't understand until she opened it. Inside, nested in tissue paper, was a small wooden urn with a brass plate: OSCAR. And a card, handwritten by a vet tech she'd never met, explaining that her ex-husband had listed her as the contact. He'd moved west with the cat after the divorce. She hadn't known Oscar was sick. She hadn't known anything; they hadn't spoken in three years. She sat down on the hallway floor with the box in her lap. Oscar had been hers first, a scrawny kitten she'd found behind a dumpster in graduate school, who used to sleep on her textbooks and bat her pen while she wrote. She'd let him go with Paul because the new apartment didn't allow pets, and because she'd been too worn out to fight about one more thing. She lifted the urn out. It was so light. She held it in both hands against her chest, and the tissue paper rustled to the floor, and she stayed there in the hallway with her back against the door.

I didn't order anything, so when the package showed up I assumed it was a mistake. Then I saw the handwriting on the label, the looping capital A, and my knees went soft. My aunt Odile. She'd died in May. The postmark was from April; it had been lost in some depot for six months. I opened it at the kitchen counter with a butter knife. Inside was a scarf she'd knitted, deep green, the color she always said brought out my eyes, and a note: Saw this wool and thought of you. Don't you dare let it sit in a drawer. Love, O. I read it over and over. I could hear her saying it, that raspy smoker's voice, the way she'd poke me in the ribs to make a point. I wrapped the scarf around my neck even though it was warm in the apartment. It smelled faintly of her lavender sachets. I stood there at the counter with my hands pressed flat on the cool surface and my head bowed, breathing in through the wool, until the light outside the window started to fail.

The parcel was addressed to his son, not to him, and Arjun almost set it aside to forward. Then he remembered there was nowhere to forward it to. Rohan had been gone eleven months. Every few weeks something still arrived, a magazine subscription, a coupon, a letter from the alumni association, and each time it was like stepping on a stair that wasn't there. This one was heavier. He opened it at the dining table, carefully, along the tape. A pair of running shoes, bright orange, size eleven. A pre-order, the receipt said, placed in January. Rohan had been training for a half-marathon. He'd talked about it at dinner, the last time he was home, waving his fork around, so full of plans. Arjun took the shoes out of the box and set them on the table side by side. They were absurdly bright, glowing almost, the laces still tied in factory loops. He touched one of the soles. Never worn. His wife came in from the garden and stopped in the doorway and saw them, and neither of them said a word.

The package was from a law firm, and inside was a framed photograph and a short letter. I recognized the photo immediately: me at six, sitting on my father's shoulders at the county fair, both of us grinning, cotton candy in my fist. I'd never seen a copy. My father left when I was eight and I hadn't seen him since. The letter said he had died in a hospice in Arizona in September, and that this photograph had been on his bedside table, and that he had asked it be sent to me. That was all. No note from him. No explanation. I sat on the stairs in the front hall with the frame on my knees. His face was younger than mine is now. He looked happy. He looked like he loved me, which was the part I couldn't get past. All those years he'd kept this by his bed, and never once picked up a phone. I traced the edge of the frame with my thumb, around and around, the glass cool and a little dusty. I didn't cry. I just felt very tired, and very small, and I sat there until the hall went dark.

Ms. Tanaka-Reyes taught third grade for thirty-one years, and she had retired in June without much fuss, just cake in the staff room and a card. The package that came in October was from a former student, the return address a city she didn't recognize. Inside was a children's book with a glossy cover, and a note: You were the only one who told me my stories were good. This is my first one. It's dedicated to you. She turned to the dedication page, and there was her name. She sat down at the kitchen table. She remembered the boy: small, stammering, always drawing dragons in the margins of his math worksheets. Benjamin. She also remembered that she'd heard, through another teacher, that he'd been very ill this past year. She opened the back cover and found the author photo, and he was thin, so thin, with a knitted cap over a bald head, smiling. The publication date was last month. She read the whole book slowly, every page, the dragons on every page, and when she finished she closed it and held it in her lap and didn't open the rest of her mail.

Kazuo didn't recognize the sender's name on the package, only the postmark from Hiroshima. Inside, wrapped in newspaper, was a small ceramic tea bowl with a crack running through it, mended in gold. A letter in careful English explained that the writer's mother had been his mother's closest friend in school, and that she had recently passed, and that among her things they had found this bowl, which his mother had made in a pottery class in 1958 and given her as a gift. They thought he should have it. Kazuo's own mother had been dead for twenty years. He hadn't known she'd ever touched clay. He turned the bowl in his hands. It was lopsided, clumsy, a beginner's piece, and he could see the faint whorl of a thumbprint fired into the glaze near the rim. He put his own thumb over it. It almost fit. He sat at his kitchen table in the gray afternoon with the bowl cradled in both palms, and the house was very quiet, and he did not want to put it down, and did not know who he could possibly tell.

The three of us hadn't been in Grandma's house together since Christmas, and now it smelled wrong, dusty and closed up, without the coffee and Jergens lotion that had always filled it. My brother Cormac took the kitchen. My sister Fern took the bedroom. I got the sewing room, which was fine, I thought, until I opened the closet and found the quilts. Dozens of them, folded in stacks, each with a little paper tag pinned to the corner. For Bridget's wedding. For the new baby. For Fern when she goes to college. I found mine at the bottom: For Niall, when he finally settles down. I'm forty-three. I never settled. She'd kept it for twenty years anyway, waiting. It was blue and gray, with little sailboats appliquéd along the border, because I'd wanted to be a sailor when I was five. I sat down on the floor of the closet with it in my lap and couldn't stand back up. Fern found me there an hour later. She didn't say anything. She just sat down beside me, and leaned her head on my shoulder, and we stayed there among the stacks.

Zainab and her brother Yusuf worked in silence through the morning, filling boxes. Donate. Keep. Throw away. Their grandmother's apartment was small, but she had lived in it for fifty years, and every drawer was full of something: rubber bands, buttons, prayer beads, recipes written on the backs of envelopes. Around noon Yusuf opened the bottom drawer of the dresser and stopped. Zainab came to look. It was full of their childhood drawings. Every one, it seemed. Crayon suns, stick-figure families, a purple cat Zainab had drawn at four, all carefully dated on the back in their grandmother's spidery hand. Yusuf picked up a drawing of a rocket ship with YUSUF FLY in green marker and stared at it. His jaw worked. He was thirty-five and an engineer, and he had built real rockets, sort of, for the defense contractor in Houston, and he had never once sent her a photograph of one. Zainab put her hand on his back. Neither of them reached for a box. They sat down on the edge of the bed with the open drawer between them and went through every drawing, one at a time, very slowly.

I took the jewelry box because nobody else wanted it, and I didn't expect anything inside but costume pieces. My sisters had already claimed the good things, the pearls, the gold watch. But when I opened the lid the little ballerina popped up and the music started, tinny and slow, that Swan Lake melody, and I had to sit down on the bed. I'd forgotten about the ballerina. When I was little I would sit on Nana's lap and open and close the lid over and over, making the dancer pop up, and she never once told me to stop. The music wound down, slower and slower, the last notes dragging out. My sister Imelda poked her head in to ask about the linens, and saw my face, and came and sat next to me. I wound the key again. We listened together. Neither of us said anything. When it ran down the second time Imelda reached over and closed the lid, very gently, the way you'd close a door on a sleeping child, and we sat there with our hands in our laps among the half-packed boxes.

Rosa and her two younger brothers had agreed to do it in one weekend, quickly, like ripping off a bandage. By Sunday afternoon they had barely finished the living room. Every object came with a story, and every story had to be told. The chipped ceramic rooster. The ugly orange lamp. The photo of Abuela as a young woman in Havana, laughing on a seawall, her hair whipping across her face. Teo, the youngest, kept picking things up and putting them back exactly where they'd been, as if he couldn't stand to disturb the arrangement. Late in the day Rosa found their grandmother's reading glasses on the side table next to her armchair, folded on top of a paperback, a bookmark two-thirds of the way in. She hadn't finished it. Rosa held the glasses for a long moment. The lenses were still smudged with her fingerprints. She didn't wipe them clean. She looked at her brothers, both on the floor among the boxes, both very quiet, and then she sat down in the armchair, and it still held the shape of someone smaller, and she let it hold her.

The worst part was the kitchen. My sister and I had saved it for last on purpose, and by the time we got to it the rest of the house was bare and echoing. Grandmother's apron still hung on its hook by the stove. The canisters still said FLOUR and SUGAR and TEA in her careful hand-painted letters. In the drawer by the sink I found her recipe cards, held together with a rubber band that snapped when I touched it, the cards spilling out across the counter. Plum dumplings. Poppy-seed roll. Cabbage soup, with a note in the margin: more salt for Pavel. That was my father. He'd been gone ten years. Lenka picked up the card and her mouth trembled and she put it back down very fast, face down, like it had burned her. I gathered the cards into a pile and squared the edges. I didn't know what else to do with my hands. Outside, the plum tree she'd planted the year we were born was dropping its fruit into the long grass, and nobody was going to pick it up.

Callum had come mostly to help lift things. He was the oldest grandson, the one with the truck. He hadn't expected to be the one who found the letters. They were in a shoebox on the top shelf of her wardrobe, a whole bundle, and they were addressed to him. Birthday cards, every year from nine to twenty-two, each one stamped and sealed and never mailed. He remembered now: there had been the fight between his mother and his grandmother, the long silence, the years when he wasn't allowed to visit. He'd thought she'd forgotten him. He sat down on the bare mattress and opened the first one. A crisp five-pound note fell out, and a card with a cartoon dinosaur, and inside, in shaky blue biro: Happy birthday my darling boy, I hope you know I think of you. He opened the next one, and the next. His cousins were downstairs laughing over some old photo album. He could hear them faintly. He didn't call down. He sat alone in the empty bedroom with fourteen birthday cards spread across his knees and his throat closed up tight.

Mr. Haddad turned the key in the lock at seven sharp, the way he had every Monday for twenty-six years, and the bell over the door gave its usual tired jingle. He flipped the sign to OPEN. Then he stood behind the counter and looked out at the empty street. Across the road the big box store had opened its doors last spring, with its parking lot and its prices he could never match. Since then Monday mornings had been quiet. Then Tuesday mornings. Then every morning. He dusted the shelves anyway, the jars of preserved lemons, the bags of bulgur, the dates his wife used to arrange in little pyramids. The radio played softly. He made coffee in the back and drank it standing at the counter, watching the door. A man passed by the window and didn't look in. At nine-thirty a woman came in to ask for directions to the pharmacy. He gave them gladly, walking her out onto the sidewalk and pointing, and when she'd gone he stood there a moment in the thin sunshine, then went back inside and straightened the dates again.

I unlocked the bookshop at nine on Monday, same as always, and found the envelope pushed under the door. Final notice from the landlord. I'd known it was coming. I set it on the counter unopened and went through the motions: lights, register, kettle, the little chalkboard sign out on the sidewalk. Today I wrote CLOSING SALE on it, and my hand shook a bit on the S. Then I went back inside and sat in the reading chair by the window, the one that had been there since my mother ran the place, and looked at the shelves. Poetry, philosophy, the children's corner with the beanbags gone flat from thirty years of small bottoms. I could still see her up on the rolling ladder, reaching for something on the top shelf and saying, There you are, as if the books were hiding from her. The first customer came in at ten and bought a cookbook. I wrapped it in brown paper, the way she always had, and tied the string, and when the door closed behind him I kept my hand on the counter for a while, not moving.

Every Monday morning Jae-sun opened the flower shop with her husband, and every Monday he'd sing while unloading the buckets from the van, some old ballad, badly and loudly, making her laugh. This was the third Monday since the funeral. She unloaded the buckets herself. They were heavier than she remembered, water sloshing over her shoes, the stems of the lilies brushing her face. She set them out on the sidewalk in their usual places. Roses on the left, carnations in the middle, the cheap bunches of daisies by the door. The street was waking up around her, shutters rattling, a bus sighing at the stop. She went inside and turned on the light and the little shop smelled the way it always did, green and wet and sweet. His apron was still hanging on the hook. She didn't take it down. She stood at the worktable and began to strip leaves from a bunch of chrysanthemums, slowly, one stem at a time, and the quiet in the room seemed to press against her ears, and her hands kept working while her eyes blurred over.

The bakery's neon OPEN sign flickered when Augustin flipped it on, the way it always did, and then held. Five-thirty a.m. Monday. The ovens had been warming for an hour. He set out the trays of croissants and pain au chocolat, the baguettes in their wicker baskets, his hands moving through the motions he'd made for forty years. On the corkboard by the register hung the newspaper clipping from 1987, BEST BREAD IN THE CITY, yellowed and curling. He had decided last night. He would sell. His knees couldn't take the early mornings anymore and neither of his daughters wanted the business; one was a dentist, the other lived in Montreal. The buyer wanted to turn it into a smoothie bar. He lined up the croissants in neat rows, adjusting each one a few millimeters, more carefully than he needed to. The first regular came in at six, old Madame Fortin, who'd been buying the same half-baguette every morning for two decades. He wrapped it for her and took her coins and couldn't find his voice to tell her. She said, À demain, and he nodded, and watched her go.

I always loved Monday mornings at the hardware store. My father used to say that was when people came in with their weekend projects gone wrong, and we got to fix them. This Monday I unlocked the door and the first thing I saw was his stool behind the counter, the one with the cracked red vinyl seat he'd patched with duct tape. Nobody had sat on it in the four months since the stroke. He was home now, in a hospital bed in the living room, and he didn't always know who I was. I sat on the stool. It creaked under me the way it creaked under him. Through the front window I could see Mrs. Ostrowski coming up the sidewalk with a broken lamp in her arms, the way she did every few months, because she never trusted anyone else to rewire it. She'd ask where he was. She always asked. I stood up, then sat back down, then made myself stand. My legs felt like they were filled with sand. The bell over the door rang, and she smiled at me, and I tried to smile back.

Imani propped the door of the little café open with the iron doorstop shaped like a cat, the one her best friend Thandiwe had bought at a flea market the week they signed the lease. The café had been their dream, together, since they were teenagers sharing a single bad latte after school. Thandiwe had pulled out in January. A job offer in London, too good to refuse, she'd said, and Imani had said of course, of course, take it. She'd meant it. Now she was running the place alone, and every Monday morning was the hardest, because Monday had been their day: they'd come in early and sit at the corner table with the first pot of coffee and plan the week, laughing at nothing. Imani poured herself a cup and sat at the corner table and looked at the empty chair across from her. Their initials were scratched into the underside of the tabletop; she could feel them with her fingers. Outside, the street was gray and wet. She drank half the coffee, and then she got up to put out the pastries, and the chair stayed where it was.

Gloria had been volunteering at the food bank every Saturday for three years, and she'd thought she was used to it. Then a family came through the line that she knew. The Hendersons, from her old church. The father had been a deacon. He'd once given her a ride home in a snowstorm and wouldn't take gas money. Now he stood in front of her table with his two kids, eyes fixed somewhere above her shoulder, holding out a reusable bag with the logo of a grocery store that had closed last year. Gloria filled it with canned beans and pasta and peanut butter, her hands moving automatically. She said, "Good to see you, Clarence," and he said, "You too, Gloria," in a voice so careful and quiet she barely heard it. The little girl was staring at the box of cereal with the cartoon tiger, and Gloria slipped two boxes into the bag instead of one. He didn't notice, or pretended not to. When they'd gone, she stood at the table holding a can of corn, turning it in her hands, unable for a moment to remember what came next.

The boy was maybe eight, and he came through the line alone, which wasn't allowed, and I should have flagged it. I didn't. He had a backpack and a note written in pencil: For the Mendoza family, 4 people, please. His sneakers were taped at the toes. I asked him where his mom was and he said, "She's working," very fast, the way kids say things they've practiced. I filled the bag. I put in extra granola bars from the stash we keep under the table. He said thank you without looking up and hefted the bag, which was too heavy for him, and staggered a little, and then walked out into the parking lot with it hugged against his chest, his whole body tilted sideways. I watched him all the way to the corner. He set the bag down twice to rest. The volunteer next to me, a retired dentist named Harold, put a hand on my shoulder and said, "You okay?" I said I was fine. I went back to stacking cans of tomato soup, building the rows very straight, and the label on the top can kept going blurry.

Every Tuesday Shlomo drove the van for the food bank, and every Tuesday his last stop was Mrs. Petrakis on the fourth floor of the old brick building on Delancey, who couldn't get out anymore. She'd always have the door open before he knocked. She'd always have something for him, a cookie wrapped in a napkin, a story about her late husband, a complaint about the pigeons. Today the door was closed. He knocked. He knocked again. A neighbor came out into the hallway, a young woman in scrubs, and told him gently that Mrs. Petrakis had passed on Saturday. They'd taken her in an ambulance. Shlomo stood in the hallway holding the box of groceries: oatmeal, canned peaches, the bran flakes she liked, a carton of the whole milk she insisted on even though her doctor had said not to. The neighbor said she was sorry. Shlomo nodded. He set the box down on the floor by the door, then picked it back up, because there was no one to leave it for. He carried it slowly down the four flights of stairs, resting on each landing.

I signed up to volunteer at the food bank because my therapist said it might help to be around people. My first shift was sorting donations in the warehouse with a teenage girl named Anouk, who was doing community service and didn't want to talk. That was fine. I didn't either. We worked side by side at the long folding table, separating cans from boxes, checking expiration dates. Halfway through I picked up a jar of baby food, pureed pears, the same brand I used to buy. My hands stopped. I held the little jar and looked at the cartoon baby on the label and couldn't put it down. It had been fourteen months. Anouk glanced over at me, then back at her pile, then over again. She didn't ask. After a while she reached out and took the jar from my hand, very gently, and put it in the box with the others, and slid a pile of soup cans toward me instead. I nodded. I couldn't speak. We kept working. She stayed a little closer to me for the rest of the shift, our elbows almost touching.

The line wrapped around the block by nine, and the food bank ran out of fresh produce by ten-fifteen. Mariana was the one who had to walk down the line and tell people. She had volunteered for six years; she knew this happened. It didn't make it any easier to look an old man in the eye and tell him there would be no more vegetables today, only canned goods and rice. He nodded and thanked her, which was worse than if he'd shouted. A young mother with a toddler on her hip just closed her eyes for a second, then said, okay, okay, and shifted the baby to her other side. Mariana kept walking down the line, saying the same sentence over and over until it stopped meaning anything. At the end of the block a woman she didn't recognize was crying quietly against the wall. Mariana stood next to her for a moment and didn't know what to say, so she said nothing, just stood there. Later, back inside, she sat on an overturned crate in the storeroom among the empty produce bins and pressed her palms against her eyes.

Lionel had been coming to the food bank as a volunteer since he retired, every Thursday, handing out bread. Today one of the regulars, a quiet man named Everett who always wore the same brown cardigan, didn't show up for his bread. Then another volunteer mentioned, in passing, that Everett had been found in his apartment. Nobody had known he was sick. Nobody had known much of anything about him, really, except that he liked rye bread and always said, Bless you, when he took it. Lionel kept handing out loaves. Sourdough, white, whole wheat. He smiled at people and wished them a good week. But he had set aside a loaf of rye, as he always did, under the table, and every so often his eyes went to it. At the end of the shift it was still there. He picked it up and held it for a long moment, the crust rough against his palms. Then he put it in his own bag and carried it home, and set it on his kitchen table, and sat across from it with his coat still on, and did not eat.

The vending machine in the hospital waiting room ate Phoebe's last dollar, and she just stood there looking at it. She didn't kick it. She didn't press the coin return. She stood with her forehead resting against the cool glass, staring at the bag of pretzels that wasn't going to fall. Behind her, the television bolted to the wall was playing a cooking show with the sound off. Her mother had been in surgery for six hours now. The nurse had come out once, at the four-hour mark, and said things were taking longer than expected, and Phoebe had heard the shape of the words more than the words themselves. She went back to her plastic chair and sat down with her mother's purse on her lap, the one she'd grabbed on the way to the ambulance. It still smelled like her: peppermints and hand cream. Phoebe unzipped it and looked inside. A grocery list. Eggs, butter, call Phoebe re: Sunday. She zipped it back up very slowly and held it against her stomach, and folded over it, and stayed folded.

I've been in this waiting room long enough to know the pattern of the ceiling tiles. Forty-two across, if you count the half ones by the window. My wife is in there with our daughter, who is nineteen, who took too many pills last night. They let only one of us in at a time. I gave my wife the first turn. I didn't think I could bear to see Ella's face yet. Across from me an elderly man is doing a crossword, and every few minutes he sighs and erases something. A child is asleep across two chairs with her mother's coat over her. I keep turning my phone over in my hands. I keep thinking about last Sunday, when Ella came down to breakfast and I was reading the paper and I said, morning, kiddo, without looking up. Did she want to say something then? Was it there on her face and I didn't see it? My eyes are burning. I press them shut. The man with the crossword asks, quietly, if I know a seven-letter word for a long journey, and I can't answer him.

Baba Kofoworola sat in the hospital waiting room in his best agbada, which he had put on that morning without thinking, as if his wife's appointment were a celebration. Now he felt foolish in it, the embroidered cloth too bright under the fluorescent lights. The doctor had said they needed to run more tests. She'd been taken away in a wheelchair, waving at him over her shoulder, trying to make a joke of it. Sixty-one years of marriage. He had never once waited for her alone in a room like this. It had always been the other way around: his heart, his knee, his gallbladder. She had always been the one in the chair, knitting, with a flask of tea and a newspaper she pretended to read. He did not know how to wait. He did not know what to do with his hands. He folded them, then unfolded them, then set them flat on his knees and looked at them, the knuckles swollen, the wedding ring gone loose. A young nurse passed and smiled at him. He tried to smile back. It came out crooked, and he looked down at the floor.

The waiting room at three in the morning was nearly empty, just me and a janitor mopping in slow figure-eights. My best friend Tobias had been brought in after a motorcycle accident. His parents were driving down from Portland and wouldn't arrive until dawn, so it was only me. The doctors had stopped coming out with updates around one. I'd stopped asking. I sat in the corner chair with my knees pulled up, still wearing his leather jacket, which the paramedics had cut off him and handed to me in a plastic bag. I'd taken it out and put it on. I didn't know why. It was too big for me, and it smelled like gasoline and his cologne and rain. One sleeve was sliced open from wrist to elbow. I kept running my fingers along the edges of the cut. The janitor's mop squeaked. A machine somewhere beeped and beeped. I thought about the voicemail he'd left me yesterday, some dumb joke about a pigeon, which I hadn't listened to all the way through. I took out my phone and played it now, holding it close to my ear.

Mrs. Achterberg had been coming to the same waiting room every Wednesday for two years, for her husband's dialysis. She knew the receptionist by name, and the nurses, and the other families who sat in the same chairs every week. There was the young man who waited for his father; the woman with the knitting who waited for her sister. Today the woman with the knitting wasn't there. Mrs. Achterberg looked at her empty chair, the one by the fish tank, and then at the receptionist, who met her eyes and gave a tiny shake of the head. Mrs. Achterberg looked down at her lap. She had brought, as she always did, a tin of shortbread to share. She'd made the woman's favorite this time, the ones with lemon zest, because last week the woman had mentioned her birthday was coming. She opened the tin anyway and offered it around. The young man took one. Then she set the tin on the empty chair by the fish tank, open, and sat back in her own seat, and watched the fish turn slow circles in the cloudy water.

The doors swung open and a surgeon in blue scrubs came out, and Valentina's whole body went rigid, and then the surgeon walked past her to another family in the far corner. She watched them stand up. She watched the surgeon say something quietly. She watched the mother's knees give out, and the son catch her, and the long low sound that came out of that woman, and Valentina had to look away. She stared at her own hands. Her husband was still in the operating room. It had been seven hours. She had read every pamphlet on the rack twice, the one about heart health, the one about stroke warning signs. She'd drunk three cups of bad coffee and not tasted any of them. Her phone kept buzzing with texts from her sister and she kept not answering. Across the room the family was huddled together now, holding each other, rocking. Valentina wrapped her own arms around herself and held on tight, and found she was rocking too, just slightly, back and forth on the hard chair, her eyes fixed on the doors.
